analysis.one_liner: Restores the FTC's power to sue deceptive companies for consumer refunds and disgorgement of profits.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 30, 2026 by Rep. Schakowsky with two Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2021, the Supreme Court ruled that the Federal Trade Commission could not use one of its main enforcement tools to force companies that cheated consumers to give money back. This bill rewrites the FTC's founding law to clearly allow the agency to go to court and win refunds, contract cancellations, returns of property, and surrender of illegal profits from companies that violate consumer protection law. It applies to cases already in court as well as new ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who lose money to fraud and deception — fake health claims, bogus debt relief, worthless money-making schemes, and similar scams the FTC polices. The FTC itself gains a restored tool to make those consumers whole; before the bill, the agency could often win a promise to stop but not money back.

how_it_helps.text: Amends Section 13 of the FTC Act so the FTC can seek permanent injunctions and equitable relief in federal court for violations of any law it enforces, restoring what the Supreme Court limited in its 2021 AMG Capital decision.
Lets courts order restitution for consumer losses, rescission or reformation of contracts, refunds, and return of property in FTC enforcement suits.
Lets courts order disgorgement of unjust enrichment — companies must surrender profits obtained through deception.
Allows relief for violations going back 10 years before the FTC files suit, and applies the new authority to cases pending on the date of enactment as well as future cases.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that engage in deceptive practices — they would face court-ordered refunds and would have to give up profits gained by breaking consumer protection rules. The cost falls on firms that lose or settle FTC cases, not on taxpayers or compliant businesses.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively to cases already pending and reaches back 10 years, which businesses argue penalizes conduct that occurred before the FTC had this remedy available.

The FTC retains other routes to monetary relief, including Section 19 actions after rule violations and DOJ referrals, so critics can argue the change is partly duplicative and expands agency litigation power beyond what courts granted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: consumers who lost money to scams get a path to actual refunds instead of just promises to stop. The costs fall on companies found to have deceived consumers, which is the point of enforcement. The main fair criticism is the 10-year lookback and retroactive application, which is aggressive by normal enforcement standards but limited to violations of law already on the books. On balance the bill is a targeted fix for a real gap in consumer protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2026 and sent to two House committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote as the 119th Congress runs out.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on July 30, 2026, joined by Reps. Yvette Clarke and Robert Menendez, for a total of three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and additionally to the House Judiciary Committee.
No further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that profit from deceptive practices are better off for now, because the FTC remains unable to win refunds in most cases under the court ruling this bill would reverse, and the bill shows no sign of moving.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firms the FTC can no longer make pay refunds

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the FTC's authority to seek consumer refunds and disgorgement of profits.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and has not held a hearing or markup; the bill has stalled there.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the additional referral and has taken no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill drew no Republican cosponsors; no votes have occurred to test the split further.

industries.industry: Businesses that profit from deceptive practices (fraudulent health products, bogus debt relief, fake money-making schemes)
industries.note: These companies currently keep profits from deception because the FTC can usually win only a cease order, not refunds. The bill would let courts order them to pay restitution and surrender gains, directly reversing their advantage.
Legitimate firms could face FTC suits with broader remedies and a 10-year lookback, but a level playing field where competitors cannot profit from cheating benefits companies that follow the rules.

analysis.trajectory: A consumer protection bill introduced with three cosponsors in the final months of a Congress, sitting without action in its committees, has little realistic chance of a hearing or floor vote before January 3, 2027; similar FTC-restoration bills would have to be reintroduced in the next Congress.
